bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)".
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution nullifies the rule titled National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) , which was submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency on October 30, 2024. The rule modifies the regulations under the Safe Drinking Water Act to further reduce lead in drinking water, including by directing water systems to replace all lead and certain galvanized service lines under their control within 10 years.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency rule issued in October 2024 that requires water systems to replace all lead and certain galvanized service lines within 10 years. The EPA rule was designed to reduce lead exposure in drinking water under the Safe Drinking Water Act. If this resolution passes, the EPA rule would be nullified and those replacement requirements would not take effect.

industries.rationale: Water utilities would be directly relieved of the 10-year mandate to replace lead and galvanized service lines if this resolution passes.
Contractors and engineering firms would lose anticipated work from the mandated service line replacement program if the rule is nullified.
Manufacturers of water pipes, fittings, and related infrastructure materials would see reduced demand if the replacement mandate does not proceed.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would cancel the rule titled National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, which was submitted by the EPA on October 30, 2024.
plain.whoItTouches: People living near whatever is being regulated.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in the air, water and land where you live. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
